extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry and drama (poets, playwrights, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for composing tragic poetry/plays (plot, character, diction, song, spectacle) following Aristotle's Poetics; covers what makes good tragedy versus epic/comedy and how to structure parts, evoke emotions, and use language and metre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of imitation — medium, objects, manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (and related arts) differ in three respects—the medium, the objects, and the manner or mode of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the medium (rhythm, language, harmony), the objects (types of persons/actions represented: better, worse, or as they are), and the manner (narration vs presenting characters acting). These distinctions determine the kind of poetic art (epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyrambic, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy must present an integrated action (not mere episodes), use rhythm/harmony/song appropriately in parts, and aim to arouse and purge pity and fear. Language should be artistically ornamented and parts differentiated by medium (some in verse, some with song).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Plot as primary element)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (the organized action) is the first principle of a tragedy: it must be a single, complete, whole action with a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic plot should exhibit unity (one action), avoid extraneous subplots that break the organic whole, and aim for a unified effect. Whoever understands good tragedy must understand plot first, because other elements serve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of Fortune (Peripeteia / Reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change of fortune (reversal, peripeteia) is a requisite to an ideal tragedy and central to what constitutes tragic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that arise naturally from the plot's causal structure rather than arbitrary events; reversals should be probable or necessary within the story's logic to maximize tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition—various kinds in which a character comes to understand previously unknown facts—is an essential element and should be used with examples appropriate to the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recognitions that are plausible and organically linked to the plot (rather than contrived). Recognition often pairs with reversal to produce powerful tragic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Denouement (Structure care)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about the complication (dêolas) and the dénouement (bots) of the plot, especially the dénouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devote care to how the plot complicates and then resolves; the dénouement must follow naturally and satisfactorily from the complications rather than by forced devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as manifestation of moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is the manifestation of moral purpose, and ethical portraiture requires that the rule of necessity or probability apply to character as to plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should act consistently with their moral purpose; idealise character where appropriate, but avoid impossible or inexplicable behavior. Character must support the action logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Deus ex Machina (no passages out of place)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Deus ex Machina (an out-of-place passage) is condemned; resolutions must not come from an external contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve the plot by arbitrary divine or external interventions that have no prior probability or necessity within the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Emotions: Pity and Fear and Catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should arouse the emotions of pity and fear and effect their proper purgation (catharsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents and character fates that elicit appropriate pity and fear; the audience's emotional experience and purgation is a central evaluative aim of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle subordinate to poetic essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacular effect is positively against the spirit of Tragedy; spectacle (opsis) is a part but should not dominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-reliance on spectacle or sensational stage effects. While spectacle is a constituent, it should support the imitation of action rather than substitute for plot and psychological depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choral Odes and Song (Melody) must be organic
rubrics_metrics.description: Choral odes and song are elements of tragedy and should be an organic part of the whole; some parts of the play are rendered with song (melody).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make choral odes integrated with the plot and dialogue, not tangential. Use musical elements where they naturally enhance the dramatic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Poetic Diction (Language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (language) and poetic diction: words and modes of speech admissible in poetry, including metaphor; diction combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose dramatic speeches following rhetorical rules; use elevated poetic language without sacrificing clarity. Metaphor and other poetic devices are permitted but must serve meaning and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Intellectual Element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the intellectual element revealed in dramatic speeches and falls largely within the domain of rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure speeches express coherent reasoning, thematic ideas, and argumentative force consistent with character and situation; thought supports the plot's moral and philosophical dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and Measure selection (iambic as colloquial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter choice matters: the iambic is most colloquial and suits dialogue; different metres suit different effects and parts of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre that aligns with the dramatic function (colloquial dialogue → iambic; other parts may suit lyric metres). Meter should arise naturally from the nature of the utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of Time (Unity of Time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun (unity of time) or only slightly to exceed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer temporal unity in tragic action to preserve probability and intensity; epic poetry does not have such time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Epic and Tragedy (differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and Tragedy agree in unity of action but differ in length, metre, and the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction; epic is narrative and has no strict time limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing form, be aware epic permits expansiveness and narrative freedom, while tragedy requires concentrated action, appropriate metre, and dramatic presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overcharge Tragedy with Epic details
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should not be overcharged with details appropriate to epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lengthy catalogues, expansive descriptive detail, or episodic additions that belong to epic rather than to the concentrated action of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite varied forms of poetic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, unite varied forms of poetic excellence in a single tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek harmony among plot, character, diction, song, and spectacle so that multiple poetic virtues reinforce the unified action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice rules for the tragic poet (craft guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules: (1) place the scene before the poet's eyes and act the parts himself to enter into the characters; (2) sketch the bare outline of the action before filling in episodes; (3) contrast episodes of tragedy with those of epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embodied rehearsal and visualization; begin with a skeleton plot and expand with episodes that serve the whole. Keep episodal material appropriate to tragedy, not epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Truth vs common reality (defence of poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic truth differs from common reality; critical objections to poetry should be answered by elucidating poetic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or crafting fiction, privilege what is plausible and poetically true over literal historical or factual exactness; credibility in fiction comes from internal probability and artistic execution.
